cards.front: An anchoring grip has four links: an outside partner, an adhesion receptor, adaptor proteins, and an intracellular {{c1::cable}}.
cards.back: The cable is actin or keratin.
cards.quote: every grip is one chain of four links: a partner outside

cards.front: Why does losing one protein weaken an anchoring junction without always making it fail like one severed chain?
cards.back: The missing link interrupts force transmission, but real junctions contain many branched chains that share and shift load as bonds release and rebind.
cards.quote: A real junction is the fuller case: many chains, some branched, share and shift the load while bonds let go and rebind.

cards.front: At an epithelial adherens junction, the chain is E-cadherin → β-catenin → {{c1::α-catenin}} → actin.
cards.back: p120 also binds the cadherin tail near the membrane.
cards.quote: work in cells put α-catenin between the cadherin–β-catenin complex and actin

cards.front: A desmosome links desmosomal cadherins through plakoglobin, plakophilins, and desmoplakin to {{c1::keratin}}.
cards.back: This is a cell-to-cell keratin chain.
cards.quote: desmogleins and desmocollins are the desmosome's own cadherins, held to keratin by a plaque of the three adaptors

cards.front: At a focal adhesion, matrix binds integrin, which connects through talin, reinforced by vinculin, to {{c1::actin}}.
cards.back: This is a cell-to-matrix actin chain.
cards.quote: Fibronectin also ties the chain into the rest of the matrix

cards.front: At a hemidesmosome, laminin-332 connects through integrin α6β4 and plectin to {{c1::keratin}}.
cards.back: Collagen XVII is a second membrane anchor beside the integrin.
cards.quote: laminin-332 is a basement-membrane laminin, and collagen XVII is a second membrane anchor beside the integrin.

cards.front: A classical cadherin usually binds the same cadherin type on the neighbouring cell, a pattern called {{c1::homophilic binding}}.
cards.quote: A classical cadherin crosses the membrane once and usually binds the same kind of cadherin on the neighbouring cell

cards.front: p120-catenin binds a cadherin's juxtamembrane tail and helps keep the cadherin at the {{c1::cell surface}}.
cards.quote: p120-catenin binds the tail close to the membrane, the juxtamembrane region, and helps keep the cadherin at the surface.

cards.front: How does talin promote integrin activation?
cards.back: Talin, aided by kindlin, binds the integrin β tail and shifts the receptor toward its extended, head-open, strongly binding shape.
cards.quote: Talin, helped by a second adaptor called kindlin, binds the β tail and shifts the integrin toward the open shape.

cards.front: PC9 carcinoma cells display E-cadherin but lack α-catenin. In calcium, what happens to their aggregation, and why?
cards.back: They aggregate poorly. Cadherins can bind outside, but without α-catenin the chain does not connect firmly to actin, so outside binding alone gives weak adhesion.
cards.quote: E-cadherin was present, but calcium-dependent aggregation was greatly reduced and the cells grew mostly singly

cards.front: Why is the statement “every integrin links matrix to actin” false?
cards.back: Integrin α6β4 in hemidesmosomes links laminin-332 to keratin through plectin; LFA-1 on white blood cells binds another cell rather than matrix.
cards.quote: And not every integrin grips matrix: on white blood cells the integrin LFA-1 binds ICAM-1 on another cell.

cards.front: How does the four-link chain predict where a skin blister will split?
cards.back: The tissue separates at the layer occupied by the failed cable, receptor, adaptor, outside partner, or deeper matrix anchor.
cards.quote: the level of a split points to the layer whose chain failed.

cards.front: Keratin 14 fails in basal epidermal cells. Where does the blister split, and why?
cards.back: Inside the basal cells, because keratin 14 is the intracellular cable that fails.
cards.quote: Keratin 14: inside the basal cells, because the cable itself fails

cards.front: Laminin-332 is missing from skin. Where does the blister split, and why?
cards.back: Within the basement membrane, because the outside partner of the hemidesmosome is missing there.
cards.quote: Laminin-332: within the basement membrane, where the hemidesmosome's partner should be

cards.front: Collagen VII fails in skin. Where does the blister split, and why?
cards.back: Below the basement membrane, because collagen VII normally anchors that membrane to the dermis.
cards.quote: Collagen VII: below the basement membrane, where it should anchor to the dermis

cards.front: One patient's skin splits below the epidermis. Can the split position distinguish a laminin-332 defect from antibodies against collagen XVII? What test is needed?
cards.back: No. Several proteins can fail near one level. Use genetic testing for an inherited defect or antibody testing for an autoimmune target.
cards.quote: since several proteins can fail at one level, naming the protein takes genetic or antibody tests.

cards.front: Why can a blister's split layer narrow the diagnosis but not identify the failed protein by itself?
cards.back: Several proteins occupy the same layer or adhesion complex, and inflammation and protein-cutting enzymes can add secondary damage.
cards.quote: The split narrows the defect to a layer or adhesion complex

cards.front: Which two lesson examples show that the four-link, calcium-dependent adhesion chain is a useful model rather than a universal rule?
cards.back: Some contacts are calcium-independent, and GPI-anchored T-cadherin or NCAM can bind without an adaptor or cytoskeletal cable.
cards.quote: T-cadherin and one form of NCAM are held to the membrane by a lipid (GPI) anchor

cards.front: Fibrillar collagen primarily supplies strength under {{c1::tension}}.
cards.back: Its triple helices pack side by side into fibrils.
cards.quote: Tissues that rely on collagen ropes for strength under tension
cards.section: The far end: what the matrix is made of

cards.front: Elastic fibres let artery walls and lungs stretch and {{c1::recoil}}.
cards.quote: let artery walls and lung stretch and recoil
cards.section: The far end: what the matrix is made of

cards.front: A basement membrane contains linked laminin and type IV collagen {{c1::networks}} beneath almost every epithelium.
cards.back: Type IV collagen forms networks rather than fibrillar ropes.
cards.quote: two linked networks, one of laminins and one of type IV collagen (which forms networks, not ropes)
cards.section: The far end: what the matrix is made of

cards.front: How do proteoglycans make cartilage resist compression?
cards.back: Fixed negative charges attract positive ions; the excess ions draw in water osmotically, creating a swollen gel that pushes back when squeezed.
cards.quote: the fixed negative charges attract mobile positive ions, and that excess of ions draws water in by osmosis
cards.section: The far end: what the matrix is made of

cards.front: How does hyaluronan differ structurally from a proteoglycan, and what matrix role does it serve?
cards.back: Hyaluronan is a long, unsulfated glycosaminoglycan without a protein core. It binds water and forms the backbone of large proteoglycan aggregates.
cards.quote: Cartilage's aggrecan binds along hyaluronan into aggregates large enough to stay trapped in the collagen net
cards.section: The far end: what the matrix is made of

cards.front: Why is the extracellular matrix more than a mechanical scaffold?
cards.back: It stores growth factors, including latent TGF-β, that can be released when the matrix is cut or pulled.
cards.quote: Growth factors held in it can be released when the matrix is cut or pulled
cards.section: The far end: what the matrix is made of

cards.front: Alanine replaces a glycine in type I collagen's triple helix. Which load-bearing tissue is especially vulnerable, and under what load?
cards.back: Bone is especially vulnerable under tension. The larger alanine side chain disrupts close triple-helix packing, weakening collagen ropes and making fractures more likely.
cards.quote: Glycine sits at every third position, where the strands pack closest, and a larger side chain loosens the helix there.
cards.section: The far end: what the matrix is made of

cards.front: How does increasing force affect a slip bond versus a catch bond?
cards.back: A slip bond's lifetime shortens as force rises. A catch bond lasts longer over a limited force range, then shortens when greater force tears it apart.
cards.quote: for an ordinary bond, a slip bond, pulling harder shortens it.

cards.front: A bond lasts 0.5 s at 2 pN, 3 s at 8 pN, and 0.4 s at 20 pN. What behavior does this show, and why?
cards.back: A catch bond over a limited range. Lifetime first rises with force, then falls once higher force destabilizes the bond.
cards.quote: Rise, then fall: short at almost no force, longer at a moderate force, short again once force tears the bond apart.

cards.front: How can pulling on talin reinforce an integrin–actin connection?
cards.back: Pulling unfolds talin rod bundles and exposes hidden vinculin-binding sites. Bound vinculin adds further ties to actin.
cards.quote: Stretching a purified piece of the rod unfolds bundles and exposes those sites.

cards.front: In mouse fibroblasts, myosin II is blocked, but engineered talin and vinculin cannot adopt their autoinhibited closed shapes. Will they still bind, and why?
cards.back: Yes. In this experiment, releasing autoinhibition exposed their sites and permitted binding even without force from myosin II.
cards.quote: engineered forms released from it bound each other even with myosin II blocked.

cards.front: A cultured cell pulls equally on two matrix-linked adhesion chains, but one gel yields more. What could the cell infer, and what limitation applies?
cards.back: It could sense that the more-yielding gel offers less resistance on that timescale. Yielding alone cannot distinguish lower initial stiffness from faster relaxation, and a culture mechanism does not establish cell fate in a body.
cards.quote: One reading is that a cell feels stiffness by pulling on its chains and sensing how much the far end gives.

cards.front: Choose an assay for each question: Do separated cells re-clump? Do cells remain on a matrix-coated surface after washing? Does a receptor contribute to either process?
cards.back: Use reaggregation, attachment, and antibody-blocking assays, respectively.
cards.quote: Classic cadherin and integrin experiments used dissociation and reaggregation assays

cards.front: An attachment assay retains 13,600 cells with isotype antibody, 3,200 with blocking antibody, and 1,000 on BSA. What is the background-corrected inhibition?
cards.back: Specific control = 13,600 − 1,000 = 12,600; specific blocked = 3,200 − 1,000 = 2,200. Inhibition = 1 − 2,200/12,600 = 0.8254, about 83%.
cards.quote: Specific attachment is 13,600 − 1,000 = 12,600 with the isotype control

cards.front: If background cells are not subtracted from both isotype and blocking wells, will a blocking antibody appear more or less effective, and why?
cards.back: Less effective. The same background remains in both wells, diluting the measured proportional drop caused by blocking specific attachment.
cards.quote: Less effective: background cells sit in both wells and dilute the drop.

cards.front: Why should an attachment assay compare a blocking antibody with an isotype-control antibody rather than only with no antibody?
cards.back: The isotype control measures effects of an irrelevant antibody of the same class, preventing those effects from being misattributed to receptor blocking.
cards.quote: An irrelevant antibody cost 2 points; comparing with the no-antibody well would credit that drop to the integrin.

cards.front: What does reduced attachment after adding an integrin-blocking antibody show, and what does it not show?
cards.back: It implicates the integrin in attachment, but does not prove direct integrin–matrix contact; the antibody could sterically block or lock the receptor inactive.
cards.quote: Lower attachment implicates the integrin in attachment; it does not show that the integrin touches fibronectin.

cards.front: After an antibody-blocking assay implicates an integrin in laminin attachment, what next experiment can test direct association?
cards.back: Use purified antigen with laminin in an association assay, such as equilibrium gel filtration, and test whether the antibody blocks that purified association.
cards.quote: the antibody blocked the purified laminin association.

cards.front: Design a test of whether E-cadherin and P-cadherin can sort cells by cadherin identity.
cards.back: Express each cadherin in a separate L-cell population, label the populations differently, match surface expression, mix them in calcium, and score whether aggregates form same-color patches.
cards.quote: Make two L-cell lines, one expressing E-cadherin and one expressing P-cadherin.

cards.front: Equal-expression E-cadherin and P-cadherin L cells form separate color patches in calcium. What does this show, and what does it not establish?
cards.back: It shows preferential sorting by cadherin identity, not exclusive homophilic binding or the strength of unlike contacts; tension and movement can also shape patches.
cards.quote: Patches show a preference, not exclusivity: different classical cadherins can also bind one another.

cards.front: Which controls separate cadherin identity from calcium dependence, antibody specificity, native L-cell adhesion, and expression amount in a cell-sorting experiment?
cards.back: Use EGTA, a blocking antibody for each cadherin, untransfected L cells, and matched surface expression measured by flow cytometry.
cards.quote: Controls: untransfected L cells (little aggregation); EGTA, which removes calcium (aggregation should fail)

cards.front: How can cell sorting be quantified instead of judged from a representative image?
cards.back: Across many aggregates and independent experiments, calculate a mixing index such as the fraction of each cell's neighbours that share its colour.
cards.quote: Score images with a mixing index, such as the fraction of each cell's neighbours sharing its colour
